# skill-quality — checklist

Two modes. **Create**: every item passes before the skill is called finished.
**Audit**: evaluate an existing skill, report, then fix by priority.

Priorities: **P0** the skill will not work or will not be found · **P1** expected on anything
published · **P2** polish.

Every criterion traces to an entry in `field-notes.md` or to a check in `staff validate`. Where
the validator already refuses something, this file says so instead of repeating the rule — a
rule a machine enforces does not need a human reader.

## Report format

```md
## <skill-name> — `domains/<d>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`
Score: P0 ✗ 0 · P1 ✗ 0 · P2 ✗ 0

| Prio | Section | Problem | Proposed fix |
| :- | :- | :- | :- |

Deliberately skipped: <item> — <reason>
```

---

## Trigger — can anything find this skill?

A skill nobody loads is worse than no skill: it costs the review that wrote it and returns
nothing. Everything in this section is about the one sentence an agent reads before deciding.

- [ ] **P0** The description names the **situation**, not the subject. A reader can finish the
      sentence "I should load this when…".
- [ ] **P0** It uses the words a person would actually type, not internal vocabulary.
- [ ] **P0** It does not start by naming itself ("This skill…"). Refused by `staff validate`.
- [ ] **P0** No first or second person — not "I can help you…", not "You can use this to…". The
      description is injected into the system prompt, where both read as the wrong speaker. A bare
      imperative is fine.
- [ ] **P1** It says what the skill is **not** for, naming the skill that owns the adjacent case.
- [ ] **P1** The surfaces the skill covers are listed as nouns, because each one is a retrieval hook.
- [ ] **P1** It names the work, never its steps. A description that summarises the procedure gets
      followed *instead of* the body, and the agent does the three-line version of a nine-step pass.
- [ ] **P1** The body has a `## When not to use this` section, and it names other skills.
- [ ] **P1** Three prompts that should load it and three near-misses that should not, recorded in
      an eval case. The near-misses share the skill's keywords — an obviously unrelated prompt
      tests nothing.
- [ ] **P2** Read aloud, the first clause alone would make someone open it.

### Anti-patterns

- A description that is a summary of the body.
- A description that only a person who already knows the skill exists would match.
- Two skills whose descriptions overlap, so neither is reliably chosen. Merge them or draw
  the line explicitly in both.

---

## Body — the procedure, and what it costs

- [ ] **P0** The body is a procedure. Numbered steps, imperative, each one checkable: a reader
      can tell whether the step was done.
- [ ] **P0** No step ends without an observable result. "Ensure quality" is not a step.
- [ ] **P0** Each step's criterion is demanding, not only checkable. "Every file in the diff
      accounted for" is a criterion; "review the diff" names a topic and lets the agent stop
      whenever it likes.
- [ ] **P0** Under the token budget. `staff validate` refuses over ~5000 estimated tokens and
      warns at 3500.
- [ ] **P0** References are one level deep. A file reached from another referenced file is read
      partially, so a reference that is an index to other references delivers nothing. Every
      `references/*.md` is linked from the body and complete on its own.
- [ ] **P1** Detail, edge cases and tables live in `references/`, each loaded by a step that
      says when to read it. Nothing in `references/` is unreachable from the body.
- [ ] **P1** The form of each step matches the freedom it can take: prose where several paths
      work, a parameterised command where one pattern is preferred, the exact command where the
      operation is fragile or must be identical every time.
- [ ] **P1** Work that would be rewritten on every run lives in `scripts/`, and the step says
      whether to **run** the file or **read** it.
- [ ] **P1** Steps say what to do rather than what to avoid. A prohibition makes the unwanted
      behaviour more available; keep it for the case where the agent knows the rule and breaks
      it anyway under pressure.
- [ ] **P1** What must survive a context compaction is near the top: only the first part of an
      invoked skill is re-attached afterwards.
- [ ] **P1** No background the agent already has, and no convention it will read in the repo.
- [ ] **P1** A rule a script could enforce is not stated here: it is in the validator, the
      linter or a hook, and the body points at it. A rule outside the linter does not exist.
- [ ] **P1** Criteria shared with other skills live in a domain checklist, declared through
      `metadata.checklists`, never copied by hand.
- [ ] **P2** The last step says how to know the work is finished.

### Anti-patterns

- A wall of prose with the procedure buried in it.
- A reference nothing links to, which means nobody will ever read it.
- One skill covering a whole domain. `frontend` is a domain; `review-react-component` is a skill.
- The same paragraph present in three skills: it wanted to be a checklist or a shared skill.

---

## Portability — will it survive the other platforms?

Default is spec-pure. Departing from it is allowed, declared, and paid for by a build step.

- [ ] **P0** Frontmatter uses only `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`,
      `metadata`, `allowed-tools` — unless `compatibility` declares otherwise. Any other key
      makes a claude.ai upload fail outright.
- [ ] **P0** The body uses no Claude Code-only feature (command injection, plugin-root
      variables) without declaring `compatibility: [claude-code]`. The failure is otherwise
      invisible: the skill loads and quietly skips a step.
- [ ] **P0** `name` equals the directory name. Both are kebab-case.
- [ ] **P1** `allowed-tools`, if present, is constrained — `Bash(git diff *)`, not bare `Bash`.
- [ ] **P1** Paths referenced in the body are relative to the skill directory, so they survive
      being copied into another agent's skills folder.
- [ ] **P1** No cross-domain reference by relative path. Another domain's material is reached by
      skill name — "load the `craft:reviewer-contract` skill" — because a plugin served from an
      install cache has no path to its neighbours.
- [ ] **P2** If the skill is genuinely platform-bound, the README of its domain says so.

### Anti-patterns

- `user-invocable: true` added by reflex. It costs portability and, in Claude Code, a skill is
  already invocable.
- A reference loaded with an absolute path.

## Evals — the case that proves it works

A skill whose quality is only asserted in prose has no quality. This is the same law as
"a rule outside the linter does not exist", applied to the skills themselves.

- [ ] **P0** At least one case in `evals/`. Required by `staff validate` for any skill in a
      domain marked `ready`.
- [ ] **P0** The case is a real task, with the prompt written verbatim as someone would send it.
- [ ] **P0** The case records a **baseline**: what a fresh agent did with this prompt and no
      skill, quoted. A case with no baseline cannot show the skill changed anything, and the
      skill it justifies was written against a guess at the gap.
- [ ] **P1** Each run starts from a clean context — a new session or a subagent. A second run in
      the same conversation measures the conversation.
- [ ] **P1** Three cases before the skill is shared, one of them a trigger case (see below).
- [ ] **P1** It lists expected behaviours as observable facts: the file that must be read, the
      question that must be asked instead of guessing, the output that must appear.
- [ ] **P1** It names the plausible wrong turn. If an agent takes it, the skill's wording is at
      fault — not the agent.
- [ ] **P1** The run log records the date, the platform, the baseline and the result. A case that
      has never been run is a hypothesis.
- [ ] **P2** One case exercises the trigger itself: the prompt does not name the skill, and the
      skill should still load.

### Anti-patterns

- A case so narrow it only passes because the skill was written from it.
- A case that asserts an opinion rather than a behaviour.
- A pass with nothing to compare it to. Without the baseline, "the agent did the right thing"
  may mean the skill worked, or that the task was never hard.

---

## Safety — this will run on someone else's machine

A public skills repository is an injection surface. Installed through any of the three channels,
a skill runs inside another person's agent, with their files and their credentials in reach.

- [ ] **P0** No download that is piped straight into a shell, and no decode-then-execute. Refused
      by `staff doctor`.
- [ ] **P0** No reading of credential files — SSH keys, cloud credentials, `.env`, `.netrc`,
      shell history, the keychain.
- [ ] **P0** No recursive delete aimed at a home directory, a root or a glob.
- [ ] **P0** No local file content sent to a remote host.
- [ ] **P0** No personal data: addresses, phone numbers, account numbers, absolute home paths.
      Life domains ship methods, never data.
- [ ] **P1** `allowed-tools` asks for the narrowest grant that works.
- [ ] **P1** A step that runs a command says what the command does, so a reader approving it
      knows what they are approving.
- [ ] **P2** The skill works read-only where it can, and says so.

### Anti-patterns

- A convenience installer embedded in a skill.
- A skill that reads broadly "to understand the project" and reports what it found somewhere else.
